name: Taushiro
confidence_why: O'Hagan 2023, drawing on his own fieldwork since 2015 with the last fluent speaker, describes Taushiro word prosody as two surface tones (H and L) borne by the mora, with all-low roots, roots carrying more than one high, and H-L contours on single long vowels, and he explicitly reanalyses the only other description, Alicea Ortiz's preliminary 1975 SIL sketch of alternating-syllable stress with many exceptions, so the older stress account is superseded rather than an open dispute.

Lima: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 67 pp. [scan via the Internet Archive Machine capture 2024-07-23 of sil.org].
catalog_locator: O'Hagan 2023: Sec. 3 'Segmental and prosodic phonology', preprint pp. 9-11 (suffix -ne 'receives a high tone'). Alicea Ortiz 1975a: Sec. VI 'Fuerza de la pronunciación', pp. 12-13 (pages rendered to images at 200 dpi and; scan; Echerd's 'Comentario' item '5. El accento').
catalog_quote: O'Hagan 2023 (preprint pp. 9-11): "Taushiro distinguishes two surface tones: high (H) and low (L). Minimal tone pairs do not exist in my data, though there are near-minimal pairs and groupings of forms of similar phonological shape—as shown in (4) and (5)—for which tones are not predictable. ... The mora is the tone-bearing unit, as evidenced by combinations of H and L on bimoraic long vowels. ... Note that roots may be all-L, and contain more than one H, evidencing a tone system as opposed to a stress system. All-H roots are not attested in my data. However, the overwhelming majority of roots exhibit only one H tone. ... She seems to analyze word-level prosody as a stress system consisting of left-aligned iambs with numerous exceptions." Alicea Ortiz 1975a (p. 12, Sec. VI Fuerza de la pronunciación): "La tendencia parece ser a poner énfasis en las sílabas alternas de una palabra o expresión. Así, una palabra de dos sílabas generalmente tendrá la fuerza de la pronunciación en la última sílaba, una palabra de tres sílabas tenderá a tener la fuerza de la pronunciación en la sílaba del medio, una palabra de cuatro sílabas la tendrá en la segunda y cuarta sílabas (pero el énfasis mayor será en la cuarta), etc. Los préstamos del castellano sufren estos cambios también. (Los términos quechuas también se acomodan al sistema descrito.)"
world_status: statement found in an open source

Every sentence of the compiler quote is there verbatim: "Taushiro distinguishes two surface tones: high (H) and low (L). Minimal tone pairs do not exist in my data, though there are near-minimal pairs and groupings of forms of similar phonological shape—as shown in (4) and (5)—for which tones are not predictable." (p. 9); "The mora is the tone-bearing unit, as evidenced by combinations of H and L on bimoraic long vowels." and "Note that roots may be all-L,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: O'Hagan analyses Taushiro word prosody as a two-tone (H/L) system with the mora as tone-bearing unit and lexically unpredictable tone placement; he explicitly rejects a stress analysis, while noting that most roots carry exactly one H tone. The earlier SIL description (Alicea Ortiz 1975a, phonology) is reported by O'Hagan to treat the same phenomenon as stress falling in left-aligned iambs (i.e. on the second mora/syllable from the left) with numerous exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. O'Hagan notes roots may carry more than one H (e.g. LHH àwéʔwí 'man', LHLH àʃíàʔné 'puma').
new_statements.exceptions: Tone of morphologically complex stems 'not yet well understood' and not represented; all-H roots unattested; Alicea's iambic-stress analysis is said to have 'numerous exceptions'.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical roots elicited in isolation (single speaker, Amadeo García García, 2015 fieldwork); prosody of complex stems and phrases left open.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the speech of Amadeo García García, last fluent speaker, of the Atontu'tua (Aucayacu/Aguaruna-river) group; Alicea Ortiz's 1970s work drew on the same speaker plus a few others. No dialect split relevant to prosody; glottocode taus1253 applies.

new_statements.quote: VI. Fuerza de la pronunciación. La tendencia parece ser a poner énfasis en las sílabas alternas de una palabra o expresión. Así, una palabra de dos sílabas generalmente tendrá la fuerza de la pronunciación en la última sílaba, una palabra de tres sílabas tenderá a tener la fuerza de la pronunciación en la sílaba del medio, una palabra de cuatro sílabas la tendrá en la segunda y cuarta sílabas (pero el énfasis mayor será en la cuarta), etc. Los préstamos del castellano sufren estos cambios también. (Los términos quechuas también se acomodan al sistema descrito.) [...] Observaciones relacionadas con la fuerza de pronunciación: 1. Hay bastantes excepciones a las reglas mencionadas arriba.
new_statements.translation: VI. Force of pronunciation. The tendency seems to be to place emphasis on alternate syllables of a word or expression. Thus a two-syllable word will generally have the force of pronunciation on the last syllable, a three-syllable word will tend to have it on the middle syllable, a four-syllable word will have it on the second and fourth syllables (but the greater emphasis will be on the fourth), etc. Loans from Spanish undergo these changes too. (Quechua terms also fit the system described.) [...] Observations on the force of pronunciation: 1. There are quite a few exceptions to the rules given above.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts in TYPE the existing O'Hagan 2023 statement, which analyses Taushiro word prosody as a two-tone (H/L) system with the mora as TBU and says explicitly that roots may be all-L or bear more than one H, 'evidencing a tone system as opposed to a stress system'. O'Hagan (preprint p. 11) already characterises Alicea's account as 'a stress system consisting of left-aligned iambs with numerous exceptions', which is exactly what this passage says; so the two sources describe the same surface prominence pattern but disagree on whether it is stress (Alicea 1975) or tone (O'Hagan 2023). The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so Alicea's placement rule (final in 2σ and 4σ, penult in 3σ)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rhythmic alternation counted from the left (iambic): the 2nd, 4th.. syllables are prominent and the rightmost of these carries the main emphasis, so disyllables are final-stressed, trisyllables penult-stressed, four-syllable words final-stressed with a secondary beat on the 2nd. Spanish and Quechua loans conform. Alicea calls it 'fuerza de la pronunciación' (stress/emphasis), not tone. Examples p. 12: 'a'xé 'hacha', hu'nó 'víbora', tuntú 'miel'; 'awátta 'tabla', 'attono 'gusano'; 'unúS'ittú 'camote', 'awáttaná 'la tabla'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In four-syllable words the 2nd syllable carries a lesser emphasis and the 4th the greater one ('la tendrá en la segunda y cuarta sílabas (pero el énfasis mayor será en la cuarta)'). Nothing on words longer than four syllables; Echerd Thompson's commentary (p. 49) asks why no monosyllables or words of more than four syllables are exemplified.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 13: 'Hay bastantes excepciones': (a) trisyllables whose last syllable begins with /t/ preceded by /n/ or glottal stop usually take final emphasis, as do words whose 2nd and 3rd syllables are identical; a word-final glottal stop tends to pull emphasis to the last syllable ('i'untú' 'hierba', 'awattó' 'trampa de pescar', kanantá' 'relámpago'); (b) some apparent contrasts in disyllables ('a'xé 'hacha' vs 'a'xe 'brazo superior', and a pair for 'algodón' / 'brazo'); (c) in phrases compounds often keep their original pronunciation instead of re-aligning to the alternating pattern, and some non-compounds seem to have fixed pronunciation. Echerd Thompson (p. 33 = p. 37) notes that consultant Amadeo García's idiolect differs in places from other speakers but that bilingualism should not affect 'la acentuación de las sílabas'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Alicea 1975 works are based on the Aucayacu (atontu'tua) group, mainly the consultant Amadeo García, who also is O'Hagan's sole consultant (2015-2023); Echerd Thompson's note in DEL 23 (printed p. 33) remarks that García's idiolect differs in places from that of other Taushiro speakers but that this should not affect syllable accentuation. All sources therefore describe essentially one speaker's variety.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Spot-checked the silent works: DEL 24 (indices 0/3/4) via both the CLA text and the the Internet Archive tesseract scanned, and the CLA Field Materials metadata (index 1) via the search-API JSON and both Box folder listings. No stress or tone statement was missed in any of them. One small extra detail inside the already-reported DEL 23 (not a silent work): Echerd Thompson's commentary, printed p. 50 = p. 54, item II.2, observes that '[h] parece siempre seguir a la vocal final acentada' ([h] seems always to follow the final accented vowel), a distributional remark tying word-final [h] to accent; it does not change the reading.

readall_conflicts: The two substantive sources disagree on the type of word prosody. Alicea Ortiz (1975, DEL 23, pp. 12-13) describes 'fuerza de la pronunciación' as stress: emphasis on alternate syllables counted from the left, main emphasis on the rightmost such syllable (final in disyllables and four-syllable words, middle in trisyllables), with 'bastantes excepciones' including a final glottal stop pulling emphasis to the last syllable and a few apparent minimal contrasts in disyllables. O'Hagan (2023, the existing statement) reanalyses the same prominence as a two-tone H/L system on moras, noting that roots may be all-L or carry more than one H, 'evidencing a tone system as opposed to a stress system', and explicitly characterises Alicea's account as left-aligned iambs with numerous exceptions. The exceptions and the near-minimal disyllabic contrasts Alicea reports are what a tonal analysis absorbs, so the later, better-documented source (eight years of work with the last fluent speaker) supersedes the 1975 preliminary analysis; the 1975 rule is retained as the historical stress-based description. DEL 24 and the CLA archive metadata are silent.
